title: Snapshots and the three areas
summary: Why version control exists, and the working tree, index and repository that every command moves files between.

steps.title: Why version control
body: Without version control, a project's history is `final.zip`, `final2.zip` and `final-REALLY.zip`, and nobody can answer *"what changed, when, by whom, and why?"*
Git answers those questions. It records **snapshots** of your whole project, called **commits**. Each commit says:
- what every tracked file looked like at that moment,
- who made it and when,
- a message explaining *why*,
- which commit came before it (its **parent**).
That gives you three superpowers you will use every day: **go back** (undo a bad change), **work in parallel** (branches), and **collaborate** (share commits with a team without emailing files).
> **Tip:** Git is *distributed*. Your laptop holds the full history, so `log`, `diff` and `commit` work offline and are instant.

steps.prompt: A colleague says *"Git stores a diff for each commit."* What is the more accurate mental model?
options: Each commit is a full snapshot of every tracked file, plus a pointer to its parent commit
Each commit stores only the lines that changed since the parent
Git stores one copy of the project and overwrites it on every commit
Each commit stores only the files you passed to `git add`
steps.explain: Conceptually every commit is a complete snapshot. Git saves space by reusing identical files between snapshots (and compressing in packfiles), but a diff is *computed* by comparing two snapshots, not stored.

steps.title: The three areas
body: Every file you work with lives in up to three places:
```text
working tree             index (staging area)          repository (.git)
files you edit  --git add-->  draft of next commit  --git commit-->  saved snapshots
<--git restore--                    <--git restore --staged--
- **Working tree**: ordinary files on disk. Your editor changes these.
- **Index** (also called the **staging area**): a draft of the *next* commit. `git add` copies a file's current content into it.
- **Repository**: the `.git` folder. `git commit` turns the index into a permanent snapshot and moves your branch forward.
Why the middle step? It lets you commit *part* of your work: fix two unrelated things, then make two clean commits instead of one messy one.

steps.prompt: Which area does each thing live in, or change?
items: The file your editor just saved
The draft of the next commit
Every past snapshot and its message
A brand-new file you have not added yet
steps.explain: `add` copies from the working tree into the index. `commit` copies the index into the repository.

steps.title: Reading git status --short
body: `git status` compares the three areas. The short form, `git status -s`, prints two columns per file:
```text
XY path
- **X** (left) compares the **index** with the last commit (`HEAD`): what *will* be committed.
- **Y** (right) compares the **working tree** with the **index**: what is *not yet* staged.
| Code | Meaning |
| `A ` | new file, staged |
| `M ` | modified and staged |
| ` M` | modified, not staged |
| `MM` | staged, then edited again |
| ` D` | deleted from disk, not staged |
| `??` | untracked: Git has never been told about it |
A file that is identical in all three areas is not listed at all.

steps.prompt: A repo has one committed file, `readme.md`. You run these commands. What does `git status -s` print? (Tracked files first, then untracked, each group in name order.)
steps.explain: `app.cs` is staged as new (`A` in the left column). `readme.md` changed on disk but was never re-added (`M` in the right column). `notes.txt` was never added, so it is untracked.
hints: Left column: index vs last commit. Right column: working tree vs index.
Only `app.cs` was added. `notes.txt` was never added at all.

steps.prompt: Continuing: you then run `git add readme.md`, and afterwards append another line to `readme.md`. What does `git status -s` print now?
steps.explain: The index holds the version from the moment you ran `git add`. The later edit is only on disk. So `readme.md` is staged-modified *and* unstaged-modified: `MM`. Committing now would record the first edit only.

steps.prompt: Match each status code to what it tells you.
pairs: new file, staged for the next commit
Git is not tracking this file
staged, then changed again on disk

steps.prompt: You staged `Order.cs`, then kept editing it. You run `git commit -m "Fix totals"`. Which version of `Order.cs` is committed?
options: The version from when you ran `git add`
Nothing: Git refuses to commit a file with unstaged changes
steps.explain: A commit is made from the **index**, not the working tree. Run `git add` again (or `git commit -a`) to include the later edits.

steps.title: Make git status -s say exactly this
prompt: `~/shop` has edits in four files and one new file. Nothing is staged yet. Run `cd ~/shop` and `git status -s` to see them.
Put the repository into the state where `git status -s` prints exactly this:
Read it column by column: the **left** letter is the index (what the next commit gets), the **right** letter is the working tree.
For `MM src/Order.cs`: stage the current edit, then add the line `// TODO tax` to the end of the file without staging it.

checks.name: git status -s matches
checks.expectOutput:
M README.md
M  src/Cart.cs
A  src/Coupon.cs
MM src/Order.cs
?? notes.txt
checks.fail: The status is not the target yet. The left column changes with `git add` (or `git restore --staged`), the right one when you edit a file.

checks.name: the staged Order.cs has the Customer field but not the TODO
checks.cmd: cd ~/shop && git show :src/Order.cs | grep -q Customer && ! git show :src/Order.cs | grep -q 'TODO tax'
checks.fail: The index copy of `src/Order.cs` should hold the Customer edit only. Stage first, then append the TODO line.

checks.name: nothing was committed
checks.fail: This step is about the index, not commits. Press Reset scenario and stage without committing.

hints: `M ` with the letter on the left means staged. `git add src/Cart.cs` moves Cart.cs there.
A new file shows `??` until you add it; after `git add src/Coupon.cs` it shows `A `.
`git add src/Cart.cs src/Coupon.cs src/Order.cs`, then `echo '// TODO tax' >> src/Order.cs`. Leave README.md and notes.txt alone.
steps.explain: Two columns, two areas. `MM` is the case that surprises people: the commit would take the staged version, and the TODO line stays behind in the working tree. `git diff` shows the right column, `git diff --staged` the left one.
